messages.author: dc6d49599b8a256f
messages.subject: Within subject comparison of parameters
parts:
Hi,

As described in the manual, it is possible to compare parameters between groups in a Bayesian manner, directly from the posterior distributions of group means (e.g. subtract mu_par between groups and plot the HDI of this difference). I wonder whether it would be possible to make within-subject comparison of parameters in a Bayesian fashion? For example, if I estimate separate learning rates for different within-subject conditions for each participant (e.g. punishment vs reward), can I compare these learning rates by directly sampling from the posterior distribution?

Thanks,
Wanting

messages.author: 4bcf82a01cf98f56
messages.subject: Re: Within subject comparison of parameters
parts:
Hi Wanting,

Yes, if the reward learning is 'mu_rew' and the punishment learning rate is 'mu_pun', you can compare the parameters by:

rew_minus_pun = mu_rew - mu_pun
HDIofMCMC(rew_minus_pun)
plotHDI(rew_minus_pun)

Best,
Young

messages.author: aae41f24a6066e49
messages.subject: Re: Within subject comparison of parameters
parts:
Hi Wanting,

In short, yes. Depending on what you are interested in, though, there are two general approaches to making this comparison: 

1) Parameter estimation will give you a quantitative measure of the difference between parameters, while
2) Model comparison will allow you to determine whether or not the addition of a parameter is valuable for your model

The parameter estimation approach is what you are referring to (i.e. estimate two within-subjects learning rates and compare the posterior parameter values), while the model comparison approach would be to design multiple models of varying assumptions and choose the "best" one. In your example, this would involve creating a model which assumes that the same learning rate is used for reward/punishment and comparing it to that same model assuming separate learning rates for reward/punishment. They can be compared using multiple methods, but something like WAIC or LOOIC (described in the manual) is most common and accepted. 

Here is a link to a paper by John Kruschke on the above approaches: http://www.indiana.edu/~kruschke/articles/Kruschke2011PoPScorrected.pdf . 

Additionally, here is an example application of the approach I think you are referring to (i.e. computing within-subjects effects): http://ski.clps.brown.edu/papers/PedersenEtAl_RLDDM.pdf

I hope this helps–let me know if anything is unclear! 

Best,
Nate
